#9762. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

#9761. [$] Added indirection allows for larger BPF programs

The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.

#9759. Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

At least 178 organizations, including several major brands, unwittingly exposed website visitors to hydra-like malware via a third-party platform.

Some of the world's most recognizable brands unwittingly became conduits for malware this week, after an attacker slipped malicious code into website testing scripts delivered by Optimizely, a platform that allows organizations to experiment with and optimize their online presence.

The attack potentially exposed visitors to sites operated by at least 178 organizations — including Zoom, CNN, Salesforce, and IKEA — to malware capable of stealing payment card details, hijacking cryptocurrency transactions, and delivering exploit kits for iPhones and iPads.

Many organizations use Optimizely to run website experiments, test different page designs and personalize content for visitors. To do this, Optimizely embeds scripts in customer websites that can serve different versions of a page or its content to visitors, track their interactions, and measure which versions perform best.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

The attackers appear to have exploited this mechanism to insert malicious code into a custom field called Project JavaScript, which allows Optimizely customers to run their own code across website pages.

British Web security monitoring service Report URI, among the first to detect the activity, documented the tampering but said it could not determine how the attackers gained the ability to modify customer projects. "We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain," Report URL founder Scott Helme wrote.

Report URI said it located and examined 1,611 unique Optimizely scripts. It found malicious code in 188 scripts associated with 178 organizations. The company has published a list of the affected websites on its site, grouped by industry sector.

Optimizely itself has said little about the incident so far besides acknowledging it and pinning it somewhat vaguely to a vulnerability in the platform's Experimentation account sign-up flow. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered," the company said.

Related:Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering

In a follow-up statement to Dark Reading, Optimizely spokesperson identified these measures as including "blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts." The company has also implemented "additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation," the statement read. Optimizely however, did not respond to a Dark Reading question on how a vulnerability in the account sign-up flow could have given an attacker write access to customer projects.

"That’s the question every affected customer should be putting to Optimizely right now," says Justin Beals, CEO and founder of Strike Graph. "They need to know how a new account got write access to other tenants' projects, which project IDs were changed and when, and whether that path is fully closed."

Until Optimizely explains the authorization failure, customers can't judge whether the company's reported fix addresses the cause or just the symptom, he says.

Related:Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

The incident is a reminder that organizations need strict controls over third-party scripts running on their websites, Beals adds. Most organizations approve a third-party vendor script once during procurement and never revisit it later. Optimizely, for instance, passed whatever review the 178 affected companies ran, and the malicious code still shipped from Optimizely's own CDN under its own certificate.

"The takeaway is that a vendor approval is a point-in-time decision, and the risk changes every time that vendor’s code changes," Beals says. "You can keep using these tools if you decide where they’re allowed to run."

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, says incidents like these show why organizations implement a browser security feature called Subresource Integrity (SRI) to verify that externally hosted files, such as JavaScript, haven't been altered before they are loaded and executed.

"The problem that we have here is that you may include a file in your website that is safe for months or even years and then, unbeknownst to you, a breach occurs within your vendor and that 'file that's been safe forever' is suddenly no longer safe," Reguly says.

SRI allows organizations to perform version pinning based on file hashes to protect against attacks like the one that went down at Optimizely. "The downside is that it requires a bit more effort and management to maintain your Web pages, which are often seen as 'set it and forget it' resources," Reguly adds.

Chris Nyhuis, CEO of Vigilant, says Optimizely demonstrates what happens when trust becomes an attack surface. "Organizations allowed a third party to deliver executable code into their customers' browsers, and that trust was exploited," he says.

The answer isn't to eliminate third-party technology but to eliminate "blind trust," Nyhuis says. "Restrict where vendor scripts execute, limit their access to sensitive data, monitor their behavior and changes, and independently validate what they're doing."

Furthermore, Optimizely also needs to explain how a flaw in an account sign-up process allowed an attacker to modify executable code belonging to 178 unrelated customers. "For that to happen, there had to be a path around customer authorization boundaries," he says. "Whether that involved broken tenant isolation, privilege escalation, an authorization flaw, or access to an overly privileged service remains to be established by the forensic investigation."

This article was updated at 1 p.m. ET on Nov. 18 to reflect a statement from Optimizely.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9758. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

#9756. Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Government-sanctioned authentication middleware is used for exceptionally important legal documents, yet it's often rife with RCE bugs.

Brazil's digital certificate system was recently found to be rife with vulnerabilities in browser extensions used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals.

That's the assessment of researchers at Bay Area Labs, who this week flagged five particularly popular digital extensions that allow Brazilian citizens and institutions to not only sign official documents, but sign them with the greatest possible degree of trust issued by their government. All five of them possessed vulnerabilities which could've allowed attacker-controlled websites to run arbitrary code on users' machines.

One can only hope that the researchers, who disclosed the vulnerabilities this week, were the first to discover them. Remote code execution (RCE) in this context could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names, and hackers to breach major government organizations (as well as professionals who manage large amounts of personal, financial, tax, and health information on behalf of their clients).

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

On Sept. 23, 2020, Brazil's National Congress enacted Federal Law No. 14,063. 14,063 laid the ground rules on how individuals and organizations could digitally sign documents when dealing with public institutions. Among other things, it delineated three tiers of trust that an electronic signature could carry: "simple," "advanced," and "qualified." "Qualified" meant that a digital signature would be equivalent to a notarized, handwritten one. It would be sufficient for high-stakes legal proceedings, like real estate transfers and electronic tax processes. And any digital signature backed with an ICP-Brasil certificate — ICP-Brasil is the country's official national public key infrastructure (PKI) framework — would be considered "qualified."

Brazilian government institutions, tax professionals, and anyone in-between who wants to provide a qualified digital signature for a sensitive legal document online can use browser extensions like Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital. Each of these tools lets official government and vendor portals read ICP-Brasil certificates, to confirm that signers are who they say they are, and put pen to Web page.

These tools will also engage with non-official websites. So if an attacker can lure a victim to their own site — or, in some cases, plant a malicious ad or iframe on a legitimate site — they can engage that victim's authentication middleware. Only one of the five extensions, CertiPlugin, had any kind of allowlist, yet it included any domain ending in ".one," meaning that an attacker would simply need to purchase a domain with that common and freely available suffix in order to perform an attack.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

The core issue endemic to each of these five extensions, and others used by other national governments, is that they allow websites to dictate the dynamic link libraries (DLLs) they load. Loading cryptographic libraries is a normal part of the way these apps work. But if they don't properly check that a loaded file is trusted? In that case, an attacker that lures a victim to their site can trigger a malware download and then instruct the victim's signing software to load that malware as if it were a legitimate library.

All five extensions' RCE vulnerabilities earned "critical" 9.6 scores in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Each of them was patched as of mid-September, but lessons remain.

Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have more than 10 million installs between them.

Among that user base are some of the most significant, high-value organizations and professionals in the country. On its website, Lacuna alone counts Brazil's Federal Senate, its National Council of Justice, its navy, and its stock exchange among its clients "who trust our work." These extensions are far from limited to major government agencies, of course. BRy advertises its work with the University of São Paulo, the São Paulo metro, and one of the country's few biggest banks, Caixa Econômica Federal.

Related:Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

Attackers could have used the vulnerable authentication middleware to infect employees at major state institutions and, in Arnott's words, "cause mayhem." As an easier alternative, they could target middle class professionals: lawyers, doctors, accountants and so on. An accountant might manage digital signing credentials for hundreds of different individuals and businesses on their single computer. An attacker with that accountant's access could then impersonate those people and companies in legally significant transactions — forging agreements, submitting false tax filings ... the sky's the limit.

"It's really interesting how these signing tools always consistently have the same critical vulnerabilities," Arnott marvels, after having found characteristically similar vulnerabilities in extensions used by Belgium, Sweden, and Qatar's governments in recent months. "Since they are security tools, you'd expect them to be properly built. But they're so often making the same mistake, by allowing any site to pick which DLLs to load. I imagine it's to reduce friction so organizations can more easily load in the drivers for hardware security tokens and readers, because the driver DLLs aren't always known to the signing tool vendor or signed properly with Authenticode. It is insane to me how many independent vendors make this same mistake though."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9755. Beyls: Wrapping up LLVM's relicensing effort

Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years.

We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...]

Today, more than 99.5% of all lines of code ever contributed to LLVM are either covered by the new license, too small for copyright to apply, or no longer in the repository.

Rather than trying to "chase the last tiny fraction forever" LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

The LLVM exception to Apache-2 Posted Nov 21, 2026 13:13 UTC (Sat) by coriordan (guest, #7544) [Link] For anyone who doesn't know (like me until 5 minutes ago): The LLVM exception: https://merlijn.sebrechts.be/blog/what-is-the-apache-2-ll... It says two things. (Based on my quick read; corrections welcome) 1. That Apache-2 licensed compilers (which insert some compiler code into the executables they create) don't create Apache-2 obligations for the programs they create. 2. It fixes incompatibility with GPLv2 by saying that, for a combined work of Apache-2 plus GPLv2 code, if an authority decides that any clause of Apache-2 is incompatible with GPLv2 then that clause of Apache-2 doesn't apply. (Which I guess they decided is fine because the places where there could be conflicts, such as patents, using the GPLv2 version isn't enough of a problem to be worth incompatibility.) So, the LLVM exception looks like a pretty good instrument.

InfoQ Homepage News How LinkedIn Built a View-Agnostic Analytics System for Modern iOS UI Architectures

Nov 23, 2026 2 min read

To address the challenge posed by modern iOS UI systems where the logical UI structure may not mirror the native UIKit hierarchy, LinkedIn engineers developed a view-agnostic analytics system build around a shared MeasurableNode contract.

As LinkedIn senior software engineer Keerthana Reddy Ragi explains, while traditional iOS analytics relies on UIView instances as the unit of measurement, modern UI architectures increasingly use flattened layouts and custom rendering systems where UI elements such as cards, sections, and containers are represented by virtual nodes that never materialize as UIViews. Consequently, analytics systems built solely around UIKit may fail to capture impressions for virtual nodes, lose logical hierarchy and contextual information, miscalculate visibility and impression duration, and attribute user actions to the wrong elements.

LinkedIn's solution introduces a shared MeasurableNode contract relaxing the requirement for every measurable element to be a UIView. A MeasurableNode exposes four properties: identity, geometry, hierarchy, and lifecycle.

As MeasurableNode is a shared contract, both traditional UIViews and virtual nodes can participate in the same analytics system. Indeed, while existing UIKit views continue using native UIKit properties and lifecycle hooks, virtual nodes explicitly provide the corresponding information to the same analytics layer.

The attach and detach methods are central to this approach, because they enable the layout or rendering system to notify the analytics system "when a node attaches, when its frame changes, and when it detaches". Unlike virtual nodes, UIKit already sends automatic lifecycle notifications to UIViews. Similarly, as virtual nodes are not directly recognized by UIKit as gesture-recognizer targets, the rendering framework must traverse the hybrid UIKit/virtual-node parent hierarchy to attribute user actions to the appropriate logical virtual node.

Ragi emphasizes that this design enables gradual adoption without requiring existing view-based analytics to be rewritten.

Teams can modernize one part of the UI without rewriting everything around it. Existing view-based analytics can keep working while newer virtual nodes use the new contract.

LinkedIn engineers encountered three main challenges developing this approach to analytics. First, the widespread assumption that everything is a UIView is embedded in existing codebases. For example, "helper code that walked superviews, visibility checks that read frames directly from views, cleanup logic tied to view removal". All these cases had to be found and updated. Second, they had to strike the right balance between short-term compatibility and long-term correctness. Third, they needed to enforce the attach/detach discipline at the framework level.

Commenting on Ragi's article on LinkedIn, senior AI prompt engineer Artien Nadal observed:

I think there's a bigger opportunity here than just making analytics independent of the UI. What if teams could automatically detect when a UI change breaks event tracking or changes what an event actually means?

As a final note, although LinkedIn's implementation focused on UIKit, the underlying approach is far from being limited to it. With many apps now mixing UIKit and SwiftUI, cross-platform layout engines, or hybrid solutions, a view-agnostic analytics model based on a shared contract has broader applicability.

#9753. GitHub Actions accepts invalid YAML

TL;DR: GitHub Actions accepts several invalid YAML productions, making it difficult (read: impossible) to parse some real-world action and workflow definitions with a properly conforming YAML parser.

This is related to zizmor#1116, which has been bugging me for a year and a half.

Last April, a user reported that zizmor was rejecting a workflow containing a step that looks like this:

Apart from the use of a multi-line flow-style string for the json: key, nothing particularly stands out about this step.

Except: it isn't valid YAML! YAML says this about flow-style nodes that are nested inside of a block-style parent collection (read: map or array):

Flow nodes must be indented by at least one more space than the parent block collection. Note that flow nodes may begin on a following line.

That means the correct syntax is instead:

YAML is a big and complicated spec, so it didn't even occur to me that this was invalid. Instead, I opened tree-sitter-yaml#36 to "fix" it. I've now opened tree-sitter-yaml#51 to revert that misbegotten fix.

On GitHub's side, I'm not sure if they have a clean path towards spec conformance here. Much of the code behind Actions is proprietary, but it seems likely that the underlying parser on their end is YamlDotNet.

Actions appears to use YamlDotNet 5.3.0, which was released in 2018. However, even upgrading to the newest version (18.1.0 as of writing) wouldn't fix this particular bug, since it's still present on that version (note the !isSingleQuoted guard).

My best guess is that a 2020 patch (YamlDotNet#467) only fixed the double-quoted form because YAML's official test suite only tests rule 8.2.3 with a double-quoted string, despite it applying to both forms.

#9752. Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

Discovered using AI, the memory corruption vulnerability affects the OpenJDK runtime and could allow unauthenticated attackers to take over systems.

A critical flaw in an open source runtime at the heart of the Java programming language allows unauthenticated attackers to perform remote code execution (RCE) on myriad Java applications used globally across enterprise organizations.

The memory corruption vulnerability exists in versions of OpenJDK, a popular open source runtime. Researchers at security startup Calif demonstrated a general proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for the flaw, dubbed "Java4Shell" and discovered with the help of artificial intelligence (AI), according to a report published Tuesday.

However, they are holding back the release of "weaponized chains for individual products" to give organizations time to upgrade to patch the vulnerability, officially tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and rated as 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, in affected applications, Calif security engineer Quang Luong wrote in the post.

Java4Shell affects the following releases: Java 17: 17.0.6 to 17.0.21; Java 21: up to 21.0.13 affected; Java 25: up to 25.0.5; Java 27: up to 27.0.1; Java 8, 8u511b33-perf, its Performance Pack build. Java 11 and Java 17.0.0 to 17.0.5 remain unaffected.

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

OpenJDK published a security advisory on the flaw, and Oracle released a patch yesterday to fix the issue in the affected versions of Java. "All Java users should update immediately," Luong recommended.

The flaw exists because of how OpenJDK decodes Base64, a common way of representing binary data as text in authentication protocols, in file uploads, and to deliver network messages.

"To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once," Luong explained. "We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory."

Specifically, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors, he explained. The bug is present in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters.

"For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array," Luong wrote. "After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array."

Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted, he added. Thus, attackers can exploit the bug to reveal sensitive memory, as the highly critical OpenSSL flaw Heartbleed did in 2014, or to perform RCE. "The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:," Luong wrote.

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Much like previous high-profile flaws before it, including not only Heartbleed but also PHP2Shell and Log4Shell, the flaw has potential to create a security quagmire across entire technology ecosystems because of how widespread the use of the vulnerable software component is. Indeed, Java "is the beating heart of the modern economy" and the third most popular programming language, powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies, Luong wrote.

Log4Shell, disclosed in 2021, affected Apache Log4j, a commonly used Java logging library, and enabled attackers to execute malicious code remotely. More recently, PHP2Shell, disclosed in October 2026, exposed critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers.

Fortunately for defenders, Java4Shell should not quite have the impact that Log4Shell did and still does, though it doesn't mean they shouldn't take Java4Shell very seriously, Duong tells Dark Reading.

"Log4Shell was very easy to exploit," he says. "Java4Shell [is] harder. However, we're comparing a 10 to a 9. They are both very bad; Log4Shell was just worse."

Related:Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

Both flaws also highlight the difficulty of identifying vulnerable components hidden within applications and third-party software used across organizations; Java4Shell is similar in this respect because it gives attackers a direct route to enterprise environments through otherwise trusted apps.

"Java4Shell is a reminder that the software underneath your applications is also your attack surface," observes Dom Glavach, CISO at application security solutions provider Black Duck.

The practical problem now for organizations "is that exposure depends on the Java build, the processor and how an application handles input, and many teams cannot answer those questions quickly, especially for JDKs bundled inside applications and containers," he says.

Because flaws like these are so deeply embedded, they may go undiscovered and remain critical security gaps. In this case, the use of AI to uncover Java4Shell potentially may have helped the industry avert disaster, giving organizations time to patch before it's been widely exploited, notes James Matchett, head of security at Cloudsmith.

"Its discovery shows how AI can uncover weaknesses in widely used software that might otherwise have gone undetected for years," he says.

Indeed, Java4Shell's discovery iillustrates how AI can speed up vulnerability discovery.

"An AI coding assistant found this bug in about an hour and a first working exploit took two more, for under $200 in tokens," Waseem Ahmed, head of engineering for cybersecurity firm Secure.com, tells Dark Reading. "The flaw sat in one of the most-audited runtimes there is. That is what discovery looks like now: cheap, fast, and available to defenders and attackers alike."

However, Matchett says the flip side is it also can help attackers move more quickly to weaponize security flaws, noting that organizations are under intense pressure to find and remediate vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them. As Ahmed puts it, "defenders now have less time between a bug being found and being used."

There is little doubt that defenders should take the Java4Shell seriously. Calif researchers demonstrated RCE in a laundry list of widely deployed Java applications in their default configurations, noting that they, too, used AI to develop exploits, Luong wrote.

The team achieved pre-authorization RCE in the following: Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Meanwhile, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker are vulnerable to post-auth RCE, they said.

"The lists are non-exhaustive," Luong wrote. "We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested."

An independent researcher also shared with Calif a client-side exploit that demonstrates how "a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own," Luong wrote.

As mentioned, organizations should start mitigations as soon as possible, with patching Internet-facing applications as the top priority, and internal apps second, Luong tells Dark Reading. Calif will wait at least one-to-two weeks before releasing any app-specific exploit code to allow for defenders to upgrade.

"Thanksgiving is also coming, [and] everyone needs a break," he says.

Organizations also can mitigate Java4Shell by starting OpenJDK with one of the following flags: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding, or -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512, Luong advised.

The second should only be applied on x86-64 hosts, as OpenJDK on ARM does not recognize it and thus won't start the system, he added.

Black Duck's Glavach recommends that organizations start their mitigation process with conducting an inventory, patching Internet-facing identity and build systems first, and staying clear of unverified fixes and fake exploits circulating online.

Secure.com's Ahmed was even more specific, advising that organizations "find every server running Java 17.0.6 or later, patch the ones open to the Internet first, and turn off the Base64 intrinsic where you can't patch yet."

#9751. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

#9750. [$] Bringing the Agama installer to openSUSE Tumbleweed

The openSUSE Project has been working on the Agama installer for four years; it was the default installer for openSUSE Leap 16.0 when it was released in 2025, and has been adopted by other openSUSE flavors as well. Now the project is gearing up to go all-in on Agama for Tumbleweed, the rolling-release edition that is meant to be where updates and new features land first. Even so, the community has concerns about losing some of YaST's legacy functionality and the impact on installing Tumbleweed on systems that have less RAM.

#9749. Held together by spare time: Reviving wiki.alpinelinux.org during PHP2Shell

Reviving wiki.alpinelinux.org during PHP2Shell · November 21, 2026

It feels like this month (and last month..) has been nonstop chaos. PHP2Shell threw a nice little grenade into an already busy month, and while that was happening a GitLab RCE took down Alpine's GitLab instance. It was a whole thing, and as frustrating as it was, I'm kind of proud to say that I got to help respond to the event and write the incident announcement. Ikke did all of the real heavy lifting, but it takes a community to keep a distribution together. Everything, and I mean everything, is kept together by volunteers lending their time and talent with no expectation that there will be a reward for the effort.

We do it because we care for the work being done. Whether it's a critical service enabling a community of tens of thousands to distribute hundreds of petabytes of data that we call "Alpine", or simply enabling a small piece of software to work for personal desires. All of it happens because someone cares enough to do the work. I love this so much, frankly. It's absolutely flabbergasting what we as a community can do with our spare time.

I enjoy giving my time to Alpine Linux, because there's a community, and because we can have an outsized impact on the world by collaborating together. It's not perfect, but it's rewarding. I think I owe my career to it in a sense. I've learned so much by simply raising my hand and being willing to give my time and learn a few new things. But there's a limit to how far you get on donated time, both personally, and as a project.

Not in the sense that it wasn't used; it gets tons of traffic and contains a treasure trove of useful information that people depend on and are excited to contribute to. But between keeping the infrastructure afloat, migrating off of Equinix to new sponsored compute, and mitigating the constant wave of problems, from scale to RCE, that plague a small engineering team trying to serve a massive consumer base, well, it's no wonder that once alice was no longer contributing, the infrastructure languished a bit. This wasn't intentional, nor was it bad. There simply wasn't spare time to contribute to it.

So in November of last year ikke asked if anyone was interested in lending a bit of spare time to fixing that problem. Naturally, I raised my hand, happy to have an opportunity to do so.

This was essentially the sum of information I got about the wiki; it was all that was really documented. And despite my eagerness to jump in immediately and lift it up from whatever state it happened to be in, it took time to get access. We had a release to get out. We were fighting to get 3.23 finished and didn't even get it wrapped up until 12/3/25! So it's no wonder that it took until 1/16/26 before I got access to the server itself to start poking around and even begin to understand how the deployment was handled.

And as you can guess by the fact that I'm writing this post in October of 2026, I did not get in there and immediately upgrade it and move on.

And I think that's important. Even if I'm only giving away a limited amount of time, I hate to rush through things without fully understanding them. There's just no way I can improve something if I don't have a solid grounding. More importantly, I actually really love spelunking inside of old systems other sysadmins have set up. Everyone has a unique flair to how they deploy something. Enterprise admins end up deploying things in a real textbook manner, and when you deal with small businesses it's usually a hodgepodge of "just get it done". I haven't had a ton of opportunities to spelunk FOSS infrastructure though! What I found was interesting in its own right, mostly because I don't think I'd have deployed the service this way.

What ikke told me was spot on: MediaWiki was a git checkout with extensions and skins vendored as submodules inside the repo. You could slot in new modules using composer, and as long as you had an appropriate underlying PHP version to work with, you were golden. But that was then mixed with actual wiki data, like images, all of it lumped together in /var/www. Very simple, but not obvious if you'd not dealt with it before.

When I got into the server, MediaWiki 1.40.0 was running on PHP 8.2 on top of Alpine 3.20, but the LocalSettings.php that controlled the wiki was generated under 1.25.3. Just to give you a sense, 1.40.0 is from July 2023, and 1.25.3 is from October of 2015! It's really neat to get a sense for how long something was tended for. Of course, our friends at the Internet Archive have been archiving the Alpine Wiki since April of 2010, and based on the main page I can tell you we've been using MediaWiki for a solid 16 years now, if not longer. I'm positive it's not the same exact server, but probably the same-ish data. I made notes about all the little important bits I found, everything from extension inventories to known issues and interesting shell snippets I found in the server's history file. Anything can be, and is, helpful when you're spelunking. Truthfully, given the age of the deployment, the public facing nature of the server, and my relative newness to administering MediaWiki servers, I was approaching the problem with the utmost caution.

By the end of February I had MediaWiki figured out, but it wasn't committed until March. And not to bury the lede, but I mean that in the most me way possible. I went through the process of setting up a clone of the staging server in my homelab. From there I worked out how to package MediaWiki itself, and then break out all of the various extensions that comprise the core system into a proper APKBUILD. After packaging it, I was no longer surprised it hadn't been done before. The core extension list alone is absurdly long, and all told we use 36 different extensions for our wiki, so this isn't even a complete list.

And given the complexity, and that this was all production infrastructure, I tried to get it merged into the community repositories before making any sort of change to the production infrastructure. Anything less wasn't really right in my mind.

But it sat, not because it wasn't appreciated, but because we are woefully close to the absolute maximum storage we can host through our CDN. Not that we weren't working on that either; I started looking into our space limitations in earnest in March, when it was a potential blocker to our ability to release 3.24 in June. I knew the package was too big to go into community, but I also didn't think leaving it in testing made sense for production infrastructure. So I turned my focus to the clearer, bigger problem and started working with ikke and clandmeter to figure out a path to archive our older distributions.

By May that problem had turned into discussions with Jason at the Internet Archive, which, as this little aside suggests, was the least stressful component of any of this. Jason is an amazing archivist, and the work the Internet Archive is doing is a massive boon to FOSS projects.

And of course, dear reader, I bet you can guess what happened next. I packaged the ia tool, built a prototype to validate we could actually migrate things, and when a prototype wasn't enough, turned it into its own tool, arkivi, which can do partial migrations and reclaim space while it migrates data. None of that merged quickly either, because, well, we were out of space and had a release to cut. But once again, I had time to donate, and I wasn't going to provide half a solution to a problem I could solve.

This might seem like a bit of a detour, but I swear it's not! We are in fact still talking about upgrading the wiki! I couldn't get the core MediaWiki package merged into a stable repo, let alone any of the extensions, which means it can't be released on a stable branch. As much as I personally trust Alpine and think we do a good job keeping edge decently stable, the reality is that it's a testing area sometimes, and it makes very little sense to run production infrastructure off of it. Or if you are going to do that, you need to ensure you have the time to keep up with the constant churn. You can probably guess my concern here: I might not have that time to give.

There are so many disparate but interconnected problems going on in the background of most FOSS distributions that you just can't fathom until you live with them. And the wild part? Nothing I've described is unique. I work within a community of clever and dedicated people who turn this type of work around on the regular. But as you can imagine, I lost my momentum on actually reviving the wiki too. I got blocked by infrastructure constraints and couldn't complete the task in what I felt was a professional and sustainable manner, so I simply waited. My small problem didn't outweigh the needs of the distribution, and there were bigger problems to solve elsewhere. The wiki was stable, it was fine.

2026-10-21 20:56:33 @ikke durrendal: would you have time to look at the wiki? 2026-10-21 21:28:29 @ikke From our monitoring it appears that at the peak, gitlab received ~50r/s, but it probably was even higher 2026-10-21 21:33:01 durrendal ikke: yeah happy to, php patches right? 2026-10-21 21:33:20 @ikke Yes, but also alpine upgrade 2026-10-21 21:35:50 durrendal yeah I can do that, I was waiting until mediawiki got moved to community, but I'll pin it to the version in testing and we can just deal with it all later, after the CDN has space. 2026-10-21 21:36:17 durrendal I think I only have access to the test instance currently 2026-10-21 21:36:25 @ikke right 2026-10-21 21:38:56 durrendal not a problem, just flagging it. I'll get testing done tonight. Heading home from work now and should have time shortly after

PHP2Shell isn't the kind of thing you leave running on a public server, and the wiki was sitting on PHP 8.2 on a branch that was already out of support. So the wiki went dark. We were forced to throw up a maintenance page and block people's access to the wiki. And of course people asked why, and when to expect it back. Like I said earlier, a lot of people depend on this resource to use our distro!

Which of course kicked off a fever pitch of building, testing, and migrating. I wasn't ready for this! I was missing extensions, I hadn't fully tested the database upgrade process, it wasn't automated, and my packages weren't in a stable repo!

But I wasn't starting from zero either. The core package had been sitting in testing since March. I had a clone of stage in my homelab, and a README full of notes about every odd corner of the old install. The better part of a year that looked like stalling had at least given me some sense of how to proceed.

It would have been nice to take the easy out at this point, but it would have been the most temporary of bandaids:

So it was four upgrades at once: Alpine 3.20 to 3.24 (we're still working on 3.25 at the moment), PHP 8.2 to 8.3, MediaWiki 1.40 to 1.46.2, and the git submodule install to apk packages. Well, there really was no quick fix. Somewhere in that stack something would break, and it would keep creating problems down the line unless the work was done in a way that made it all easier to maintain long term.

Even if I wanted to take the quick path and just get the job done, that's the sort of logic that results in the same sort of languishing. Just run the old stuff, just upgrade the existing thing, keep it all similar, move onto the next thing. Sideload 1.46 the old way, get it up tonight, clean it up "later". I have so little time to give, and so many other important changes that need to be made. For anyone paying attention, that's only getting worse with the literal waterfall of RCEs being announced day after day after day, and we're expected to just keep up with it all. It's a lot, but it will only be worse if we cut corners and stop caring about doing it right. "Later" is exactly how the wiki got here in the first place.

Plus, that's not who I am. No, I'd rather dogfood a new tool I've been working on, finish the packaging work, and prove out that everything can and will work on a v3.24 mock and provide a good stable experience. Anything less would be unprofessional, an affront to the craft, or at the very least to my sense of pride.

Which leaves just one awkward bit. Despite all of my effort, the mediawiki packages are still making their way through testing. The work is never truly finished, there's always one more thing that needs to be done. But I'm confident once everything catches up the path forward is that much easier. Every mediawiki component and extension packaged provides a simpler maintenance path going forward. Nobody needs to remember anything I've described thus far. And anyone who wants to suggest an extension to make the wiki better can actively contribute to that process by packaging and testing it.

It turns out that emergencies are great times to stress test the library coverage of a configuration management tool, especially when you need to spin up a box, test a migration, and repeat it over and over. I could have done all of this with some shell scripts or with Salt, but it's a lot more fun to use scio and figure out how well the little Lua DSL I've put together maps onto things I'd either do by hand or know well enough another way. The reps are the point. Every time something broke, I fixed it in the state, threw the box away, and ran it again from nothing, until a fresh Alpine 3.24 container could become a working wiki without me touching it. If you're curious what that looks like, the full scio state is here.

If I as a contributor only have so much time to give, and my standard is that it's done well and to the best of my abilities, well, then I'll combine pleasure and work and solve two problems in one go. Servers get upgraded, I get a production grade test case for my configuration management system, and the entire thing is held together by spare time and tenacity!

I'll write more about scio in the near future. There's a lot to say, but now's not the time.

Did I mention I try to be meticulous? All of the preflight work isn't nearly enough when working with production infrastructure; I wanted to know exactly what I was touching. So naturally, I wrote a quick diff script to compare stage and prod, and the answer I got in the process was very reassuring. The two servers were nearly identical. The only real difference was prod's exposure layer, with go-away out front and nginx listening behind it. Then I wrote a backup script, because the existing backups weren't something I was willing to bet on. My process was obvious afterward: a throwaway incus container restored from a prod dump first, then stage, and only then prod.

Good thing, too. I could see every place I might trip, and I still managed to stumble.

First up was LocalSettings.php. Remember that file generated back in 2015 under 1.25.3? It had been carried forward through every upgrade since, collecting settings MediaWiki removed years ago ($wgScriptExtension, $wgDBmysql5, $wgUseTeX, $wgShowIPinHeader, $wgSquidServers) and path overrides pointing into a git tree that was about to stop existing. It fell over one dead path at a time. Fix a line, run the update, watch it die on the next one. Eventually I stopped playing whack-a-mole and just started over from scratch. A decade of "it still works, don't touch it", gone. I'll try my best to remember to leave a note for the next sysadmin who comes after me.

Even then, once I could actually open a page on the wiki, every image on it came back with "Error creating thumbnail: File missing." The old backups had never included uploads. The database was covered, but as far as the backups were concerned, every image anyone had ever uploaded to the wiki existed in exactly one place. Nobody was careless here. In the old install the uploads sat right alongside everything else in /var/www, and I hadn't understood where things lived well enough to notice they were missing from the backups. My mock tests never checked for them either. What an obvious and embarrassing look it would have been if I hadn't caught it on staging first!

But then I fucked up. On stage, I ran php maintenance/run.php install instead of update. It was late, it must have been nearing 1am or 2am at this point, and I wasn't fully paying attention. I should have stopped and rested, it could have waited another day, but I had committed to fixing this. If it's not obvious, install is for empty databases. Pointed at a real one, it overwrites an existing db with a fresh schema and admin account right on top of everything that's already there. Thank goodness I had a backup. I was able to easily restore the dump, put things back the way they were, start the whole thing over.

The rest were the kind of thing that just ate time, and they make for a pretty dull story. $wgMainCacheType = CACHE_ACCEL needs php83-pecl-apcu, and opcache doesn't count. The 3.24 mariadb client refuses non-TLS connections by default, so everything needed --skip-ssl initially. The packaged php-fpm listens on a unix socket rather than 127.0.0.1:9000, which I learned by way of 502s. Restored pages rendered stale, because their old page_touched values were older than the freshly built parser cache, which $wgCacheEpoch fixed. And AbuseFilter's grants were redacted in the capture I was working from, so I recovered them from the backup.

When it finally came together, the schema update on stage took 28 seconds. After all of that effort, 28 seconds.

2026-10-23 10:00:21 ncopa durrendal: are you still working on wiki.a.o? 2026-10-23 11:34:07 durrendal ncopa: yeah sorry for the radio silence, also scrambling at work over this. I should be able to finish it today though, I'll keep you posted. 2026-10-23 11:34:19 ncopa thank you!

That radio silence was the day job. PHP2Shell didn't just land on Alpine, it landed on everyone, and I spent my days scrambling over the same bug I was fixing for the wiki in the evenings.

By the time I sat down with prod, the hard part was over. It had become routine and easy because I put the learning up front where it belonged. Prod got a maintenance mode, a flag file that nginx checks on every request. Touch it and the world sees a maintenance notice, while requests from the box itself still reach the wiki, so I could test everything from localhost before anyone else could see it. Then the same migrations I'd already run on stage, with no surprises this time. Rsync the uploads into /var/lib/mediawiki/images. Carry over the parts of prod that make it prod: minor tweaks to php-fpm for performance, go-away, the easy stuff.

2026-10-24 02:40:57 durrendal ikke ncopa the production wiki is fully upgraded and back online! 2026-10-24 02:41:12 durrendal https://wiki.alpinelinux.org/wiki/Special:Version 2026-10-24 02:48:22 lotheac nice! 2026-10-24 02:57:20 durrendal thanks :) and it's using packages instead of the old git submodule install too so hopefully this shouldn't languish ever again 2026-10-24 02:57:57 durrendal I just need to open a few MRs now

The wiki is on Alpine 3.24, MediaWiki 1.46.2, and PHP 8.3, and every piece of it comes from apk. Which means the next time a PHP2Shell comes along, the fix is apk upgrade, run.php update, and a php-fpm restart. No submodules or composer, nobody needs to remember something special, all that's needed is a bit of Alpine specific systems administration knowledge and we're golden. This will get better as I finish documenting the new installation, so that when I inevitably run out of spare time, the next person to raise their hand can stand on my shoulders and reach a little higher.

Look, at the start of this I said there's a limit to how far you can get on donated time. I meant that, but not to signal some kind of fundamental flaw in the system. Alice tended to this before me, ikke kept it running alongside everything else, and when it needed someone, someone raised their hand. This time it was me. There are many, many people like me, what I've described is not unique. But look what it took, eleven months from "anyone want to help maintain the wiki?" to an actual upgrade, most of it spent trying to solve other problems around the one that was volunteered for. When the emergency came, it got fixed because someone was willing to pay down the technical debt all at once.

That's what spare time can carry, and it's a lot. It's also why it matters that Alpine is choosing to fund dedicated infrastructure engineering. Not because volunteers can't do the work, but because the work shouldn't depend on whether someone happens to have a free evening when the next CVE drops. Spare time built this wiki, and spare time will keep tending it. It just shouldn't have to hold it together alone.

As for me, I got what I always hope to get from raising my hand, an opportunity to learn. I walked in knowing very little about Mediawiki administration, and while I wouldn't call myself an expert from one small engagement, I'm happy to have come away with a few more packages, more confidence in scio, and a once more working wiki for Alpine. And a great reminder that part of giving your spare time is knowing when to stop, nobody will ever be mad that you ran out of spare time.
